results.title: July 2026 AI Selloff: Surviving the Sector Rotation | ClaritX
highlights: Investors are intensely questioning AI infrastructure costs because the immense capital required to sustain next-generation compute clusters is beginning to outpace near-term revenue generation expectations. As of mid-2026, the market is shifting from simply cheering top-line growth to demanding sustainable profitability across the entire AI hardware ecosystem. According to Tenzing Memo (July 2026), the hourly rental price for flagship data center GPUs fell notably over the summer, dropping roughly 31% in a span of three weeks. This specific pricing decline suggests that raw computing supply might currently be built faster than new enterprise workloads can absorb it. When end-user pricing falls while underlying manufacturing costs—like TSMC's multi-billion dollar capex hikes—continue to rise, the math for future margins suddenly looks highly compressed. Consequently, retail and institutional traders alike are rapidly trimming exposure to heavily leveraged infrastructure plays, fundamentally reassessing how much capital hardware companies must burn just to maintain their competitive advantages in this maturing artificial intelligence cycle.

results.title: CoreWeave, and the Question of Whether the Shortage Lasts
highlights: Five years ago a data center was mostly a software business housed in a building. The value sat in the code, and the concrete and steel were a cost you tried to keep down. Then large models arrived, needed somewhere physical to run at a scale nobody had built for, and the scarce thing quietly changed. It stopped being the model and became the place to plug it in. CoreWeave is the clearest way to own that change, and it is also a hard company to hold, because the same features that make it valuable today could work against it in a few years. I want to walk through why it exists, why the largest companies in the world rent from it even when they have their own compute, why NVIDIA funds it, and what has to stay true for it to work. Renting compute is not one business. At the bottom is colocation, the Equinix and Digital Realty layer, which rents you space, power, and cooling while you bring your own machines. Those companies are landlords of the building, not of the computer. At the top is the hyperscaler, the Amazon, Microsoft, and Google layer, which rents you a whole software economy, hundreds of managed services with raw compute as one item on a long menu, built to serve millions of small, mixed customers at once. CoreWeave sits in the middle, and the middle barely existed before 2023. It rents you an operated GPU supercomputer, tuned for one job, available the week the newest chips ship. Not the room, and not the full software cloud, but the machine itself, run for you. This is why the easy comparisons mislead. A colocation provider rents you the room, and a bitcoin miner had the power, but neither of them, on its own, wires tens of thousands of the newest chips into a single working computer and keeps it running. That operation is the product, and it is harder than it sounds. A frontier training run is one computation spread across all those chips, which have to talk to each other at full speed, stay in step, and survive individual chips failing without restarting the whole job. General clouds were designed for the opposite, many small tenants kept apart on shared hardware. CoreWeave was designed for the one large tightly coupled job, and it was the first operator in the world to stand up NVIDIA's newest Vera Rubin generation, which it did on borrowed money. Here is the question that stops most people. If Amazon and Microsoft already have vast compute, why does a frontier lab use CoreWeave at all? OpenAI is partnered with Microsoft. Meta builds its own data centers. Why would either rent from a specialist? The answer is that it is not one instead of the other. It is all of them at once. OpenAI did not go to CoreWeave rather than Microsoft. It went to CoreWeave in addition to Microsoft, in addition to Oracle, and in addition to building its own, because its total need for compute is larger than any single supplier can deliver on the timeline it needs. Seen as addition rather than substitution, the behavior makes sense. The reason is a physical shortage, and the binding constraint is power. Connecting a new data center to the grid can take three to four years, and the large transformers that step the power down have lead times about as long. So even a company worth trillions of dollars has a ceiling on how many gigawatts it can bring online in a year, and a top lab's need over the next two to three years runs past what its main partner can build in time. The gap is measured in gigawatts, and it is real. CoreWeave exists to fill it. The proof sits in the two facts that look like contradictions. OpenAI committed on the order of twenty-two billion dollars to CoreWeave even though Microsoft is its closest partner, and Meta committed about twenty-one billion even though it builds its own fleet. When the two companies with the deepest access to compute still rent tens of billions from a specialist, it tells you that partner-supply and self-supply were not enough during the ramp. Building your own takes years, and the compute is needed now, so a lab rents bridge capacity from whoever can energize it first. That leaves why CoreWeave can add capacity faster than Microsoft can. Two reasons. The first is focus, since it folds new chips into a single-purpose build rather than a giant general fleet under enterprise constraints. The second, and the larger one, is a willingness to take balance-sheet risk. A hyperscaler will not bet its balance sheet on graphics cards at three times leverage, and CoreWeave will. It borrows tens of billions against its contracts to buy chips and power ahead of the revenue, so what it sells is speed bought with debt, capacity that exists two to three quarters before the incumbent's version would. People often reach first for a neutrality argument, that a lab uses a specialist so a competitor cannot see its work. There is something to it, but I would put it second. The isolation on a hyperscaler is strong, so this is less about a rival copying your model and more about two plainer things, negotiating leverage, because a lab that depends on one partner is owned by it at every renewal, and not wanting the whole company gated by one partner's build schedule. Neutrality is the tiebreaker rather than the driver, and the driver is scarcity and speed. This connects to a question people find strange. NVIDIA has invested in CoreWeave, gives it early access to chips, and puts it on stage next to Nebius. Why fund and promote your own customers? Because it is a supplier strategy. NVIDIA's three largest customers, the hyperscalers, are also its three largest long-run risks, because each is designing its own AI chip to depend less on NVIDIA. Google has the TPU, Amazon has Trainium, Microsoft has Maia, and every dollar spent on those is a dollar not spent on NVIDIA. Neoclouds are the counterweight. They buy only NVIDIA, they have no in-house silicon program, and when NVIDIA gives one of them early allocation it is seeding a demand channel that stays aligned with its roadmap and keeps the market from consolidating under the buyers most motivated to replace it. The counterpoint belongs right next to this. NVIDIA invests in CoreWeave, CoreWeave uses that money and its debt to buy NVIDIA chips, and those purchases flatter NVIDIA's revenue. The end demand from the labs is real, so it is not a mirage, but the loop does make the growth look cleaner than a fully arms-length market would. Now the hard part. NVIDIA releases a new generation roughly every year, and CoreWeave makes each one available almost at once, which is its appeal. But what happens to the chips it already owns? They do not become worthless. When the newest generation takes over frontier training, the previous one moves down to less demanding work, running production inference, then smaller models, each step a lower price but still a paying tenant. In a market this short on compute, even old chips keep earning. The catch is that the scarce input is not the chip. It is the power. Picture a data center as a garage where each space is one megawatt and the number of spaces is fixed. You want each space filled with the machine that earns the most. When a new generation does roughly twice the useful work per megawatt, the old chip in that space now earns half of what the space could, so the chip is not broken, it has simply been out-earned, and you would rather pull it and install a new one. The pressure to replace runs stronger than whether the chip still works, which is why the competitive life of a chip is shorter than it looks. This is where the accounting matters. The industry depreciates these chips over roughly five to six years. If the real economic life for competitive work is closer to two to three years, then spreading the cost over six years records too little depreciation each year and makes reported profit look better than the cash economics. The criticism is fair to weigh. It does not mean the chips are worthless in year three, only that the earnings likely flatter the picture. You can see the tension in two numbers CoreWeave reports. Its adjusted profit margin, the figure management leads with, is about 56 percent, and its free cash flow margin is about negative 170 percent. The distance between them is depreciation and interest, so the 56 percent leaves out the cost of the treadmill, and the gap between the two figures is what running that treadmill costs. That raises the follow up question. CoreWeave borrows enormous sums to buy chips, so does it have to clear that debt before it earns anything, and how much room is left for profit? No. A leveraged infrastructure company rolls its debt, grows into it, and lives on the spread. Walk the layers on the case where CoreWeave reaches about twenty-one billion dollars of revenue. Adjusted profit at 56 percent is about twelve billion. Subtract depreciation, the chips wearing out, which on a fleet this size is roughly twelve to fifteen billion a year, so depreciation alone is close to the entire margin. Subtract interest, about four billion a year on some forty billion of debt, and the accounting result lands near breakeven, which is why a company growing revenue over one hundred percent still reports losses. Cash is a different story, and it is the thesis. Depreciation is not a check written this year, so the cash the business generates is the adjusted profit minus the cash interest, roughly eight billion, and that is real. Against it sits the capex, which runs above thirty billion a year and outweighs everything. Even if it eases toward twenty billion, eight billion of operating cash minus twenty billion of capex is still deeply negative, and the gap is funded by more debt and by customer prepayments. So free cash flow turns positive not when the debt is cleared but when operating cash finally exceeds capex, which happens when revenue scales far enough or the company slows its building. Today it spends about two and a half to three times its revenue on capex, so the crossover is a couple of years out at best. What improves in the meantime is the ratios, leverage falling from around six times profit toward three and a half as the backlog converts, and interest coverage rising from close to two times toward three. So the question is not whether CoreWeave is a good operator. It is a good one. It stood up the newest hardware first, it holds real contracts with demanding customers, and its backlog is near one hundred billion dollars. The question is whether the middle layer it occupies is a durable category or a shortage-era opening that the giants slowly close once they catch up on power and speed. Four things have to hold for the good case. The backlog has to convert to revenue on schedule. The depreciation assumptions have to be roughly right. Interest rates have to stay put rather than raising the cost of the debt. And growth capex has to ease so operating cash can get ahead of it. If all four hold, the spread widens, leverage falls, free cash flow crosses positive in a couple of years, and CoreWeave becomes an investment-grade infrastructure operator rather than the boom's most leveraged expression. If any slips, depreciation and interest consume the margin, the cash barely covers the coupons, and the equity is the thin slice left on a very large asset base. The first sign of the harder case has already appeared. Meta is reported to be building a business to resell its own spare compute, which is the shortage showing its first crack, because a customer with capacity to sell is telling you the scarcity may not last as long as the backlog implies. It does not break the contracts already signed, but it puts a question under the next round. I think CoreWeave is a good operator of a substitutable service, which is a smaller and more fragile thing than an indispensable one, and it should be owned as such, in modest size, with the leverage respected. The bet, if you own it, is narrow. You are betting that the shortage lasts long enough, and the backlog converts fast enough, that CoreWeave reaches self-funding free cash flow before the hyperscalers close the speed gap and the scarcity that created the middle layer fades.

results.title: SpaceX is quietly building an AI compute business that may become key to its eye-popping valuation | Fortune
highlights:
Under pressure by analysts to justify its eye-popping valuation, SpaceX is diversifying beyond rockets and satellites to a seemingly innocuous but lucrative business opportunity: renting out the unused computing capacity from its Colossus data center complex.

In May, SpaceX agreed to give Anthropic access to roughly 325,000 Nvidia GPUs across its Colossus data centers for $1.25 billion per month. Weeks later, it struck a similar agreement to provide Google with about 110,000 GPUs for $920 million per month. Together, the two contracts could generate about $26 billion for the company annually—more than SpaceX’s entire revenue last year.

...

The business model works because demand for AI compute continues to outpace supply as the AI race heats up and companies build increasingly powerful models. Meanwhile, building a large data center can require years of development and a large investment.

This makes SpaceX’s offering attractive right now, and allows it to charge a premium to customers that need that computing power immediately, Cray told Fortune.

...

This caveat could be a blessing and a curse, warned Sridhar Tayur, a professor of operations management at Carnegie Mellon University. Built into the contracts with Google and Anthropic is a 90-day cancellation provision that gives SpaceX the ability to reclaim its compute if Grok’s needs suddenly increase. 

But the same clause could also allow its customers to walk away if cheaper compute capacity becomes available, raising the risk that the revenue from this business could be temporary.

...

How lasting that business could be will depend on whether the shortage of AI infrastructure persists. OpenAI is working with partners through the Stargate initiative announced last year to build a large network of data centers across the U.S. to aid AI development.

results.title: Why AI Tokens Could Become Significantly Cheaper If the Bubble Bursts — Even Though Providers Are Already Selling “Below Cost”
highlights:
However, a large portion of the “cost” that providers are failing to cover is the depreciation or rental cost of hardware purchased or contracted at NVIDIA’s inflated prices. When providers say they are operating below cost, they are typically including these high capitalized or contracted expenses. Electricity and other variable operating costs are real but represent a much smaller share of the total.

...

Once a GPU cluster is built and paid for (or under a sunk-cost contract), the marginal cost of running additional inference is dominated by:

- Electricity (and cooling/PUE overhead).
- Minor incremental maintenance and networking.

Estimates put electricity at roughly $0.20–$0.30 per hour per H100-class GPU under typical data center conditions — a tiny fraction of the $2–$4+ per hour effective rental or depreciation rates seen in the market.

In a post-bubble scenario, several forces align to push effective costs (and thus competitive prices) downward:

1. NVIDIA’s premium compresses. Increased competition from AMD, custom ASICs from hyperscalers (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium/Inferentia, Microsoft Maia, etc.), Chinese alternatives, and potentially new entrants would erode NVIDIA’s ability to maintain 8–10x markups. Gross margins on chips would fall toward more normal semiconductor levels.

2. Existing hardware gets run harder at marginal cost. Billions of dollars worth of GPUs are already deployed or on order. In a downturn or oversupply situation, owners (or distressed sellers) will run this hardware to recover any contribution margin above pure variable costs (mainly power). This is classic economics: price toward marginal cost when there is excess capacity and fixed costs are sunk.

3. Distress and secondary markets emerge. Used or ... Cloud spot and secondary-market pricing would reflect this.

results.title: xAI Becomes the Frontier's Landlord as Google and Anthropic Rent Colossus — The Compute
highlights:
Buried in the regulatory filings that accompanied SpaceX's public debut are two leases that quietly redraw the map of frontier compute. Anthropic has taken exclusive capacity at the Colossus 1 data center for inference, agreeing to pay roughly $1.25 billion per month for three years. And Google has agreed to lease about 110,000 GPUs and related infrastructure at Colossus 2 for approximately $920 million per month — around $30 billion in total, running from October 2026 through June 2029.

Add them up and two of the most formidable AI operations on earth are committing something in the neighborhood of $2.2 billion a month to a data center owned by xAI, the maker of Grok and now a subsidiary of SpaceX. Musk built Colossus to train models that compete with Gemini and Claude. He is now collecting rent from both.

...

The Colossus campus is the largest single-site AI installation in the world: roughly 2 gigawatts of capacity and about 555,000 NVIDIA GPUs, bought for approximately $18 billion. That is an enormous fixed asset, and fixed assets want to be filled. The IPO disclosures suggest xAI has worked out that the fastest way to monetize a hyperscale build is not only to run your own training jobs on it — it's to lease the silicon to whoever will pay.

The timing matters because xAI is bleeding. The company lost $2.4 billion in the quarter ending March 2026, up from $936 million a year earlier. Against that, an annualized lease book approaching $26 billion from Google and Anthropic alone is not a rounding error — it is the difference between a cash furnace and a business. The merger that folded xAI into SpaceX valued the combined entity at $1.25 trillion, and the leases help explain how that number was defended: Colossus is no longer just a cost center for training runs. It is a compute REIT with a rocket company attached.

...

The pricing environment corroborates the squeeze. On Polymarket, bettors put the odds that B200 rental prices rose in July at 90%, with H200 at 86% (thin volume, point-in-time sentiment). When rental rates climb and the newest silicon is still scarce, owning 555,000 installed GPUs starts to look less like a liability and more like beachfront property.

There is a strategic risk here that the filings don't spell out. A frontier lab that rents its inference capacity from a competitor is, in some sense, handing that competitor a live read on its demand curve. Anthropic running Claude inference on Musk's hardware is a trust exercise as much as a lease. But when the alternative is not shipping — because the electrons, the interconnects, and the racks simply aren't available anywhere else — the calculus changes. In a compute famine, you rent from the enemy.

results.title: AI Chip Shortage: GPUs, Memory, and the Supply Chain Crisis - Global 1 News
highlights:
I've been watching this for the last eighteen months, and in the last quarter the situation went from "tight" to "genuinely alarming." We're looking at GPU lead times of 36 to 52 weeks for data-center class hardware. Blackwell orders that weren't placed by early 2026? Looking at Q1 2027 delivery windows. That's not a supply constraint — that's a structural inability to manufacture fast enough. And the memory situation is somehow even worse.

...

Let's start with the obvious one because the numbers are so big they've stopped being abstract. Data-center GPU lead times now stretch 36 to 52 weeks. If you didn't get your Blackwell B200 orders in by February 2026, you're looking at next year. CoreWeave, one of the biggest GPU rental providers, is raising prices over 20% and demanding longer contract terms. Companies that built their entire business model around renting NVIDIA compute are suddenly finding those margins crushed.

But here's where it gets interesting — and where the story stops being about GPUs and starts being about everything else. NVIDIA is reportedly cutting discrete gaming GPU production by 30 to 40 percent in the first half of 2026 to manage VRAM shortages. The same GDDR7 memory chips that go into RTX 5090s are being prioritized for data-center GPUs because the margins are better. The result? An RTX 5090 that's supposed to be a $1,999 card is sitting on shelves at $2,800 to $3,000 — if you can find one. And NVIDIA might skip a whole generation of gaming GPU launches, which would be the first time in three decades they've done that.
